**Supporting evidence:**

- MultiLLR defines anomalies as departures from month-day climatology (1981–2010) and attributes skill improvements to seasonally local anomaly modeling.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.0">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

- AutoKNN similarly operates on anomalies defined relative to day-of-year climatology and uses lagged anomaly structure for skill; analog selection uses preceding anomaly sequences.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.1">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

- Chabot-Couture constructs dew-point anomalies by removing Fourier seasonal harmonics before kriging, arguing that anomaly kriging improves interpolation by removing systematic seasonal structure.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- A climatology baseline is explicitly used as a benchmark in long-horizon climate prediction studies because it captures the mean seasonal state but not weather anomalies, motivating anomaly-focused modeling when the goal is day-to-day reconstruction.  <paper entityId="paper-55c337acba10da6961c31c4504f3748b8641c0a3" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="278327193" artifactId="extraction-result-17#uuid-e17.1">Gallusser et al., 2025</paper>

content.title: Wide day-of-year pooling as a bias–variance optimum for smooth seasonal coupling

content.text: If the Tmin–dew point relationship changes gradually through the year, pooling many nearby days gives more stable coefficients and better predictions than fitting tiny seasonal windows.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Chabot-Couture smooths day-of-year variogram and lapse-rate parameters using 31-day sliding windows (median then mean) to stabilize noisy daily fits, explicitly motivating broad pooling for robustness.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- MultiLLR uses a 56-day day-of-year window for locality, described as balancing seasonal specificity and sample size; this is an explicit broad-window choice in a successful local regression framework.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.0">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

- AutoKNN uses a 56-day day-of-year restriction for precipitation analogs (strong seasonality) but uses all dates for temperature, illustrating that broader pooling can be preferred when seasonal phase-locking is weaker and relationships are more uniform across the year.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.1">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

- STEAD explicitly adopts a two-scale regularization strategy (global monthly RVs feeding local daily fits) to reduce overfitting/noise in localized reconstructions, consistent with a general bias–variance rationale for broad pooling.  <paper entityId="paper-7989b73600c90b993f7f95e950264be5aaf91f40" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="284273775" artifactId="extraction-result-14#uuid-e14.0">Serrano‐Notivoli et al., 2019</paper>

- If the reconstruction is refit with progressively narrower day-of-year windows, cross-validated error should increase first in sparse-data zones (high Andes, arid coast) and then in all zones, consistent with variance-dominated overfitting.
- Within each climate zone, estimated Tmin-anomaly→Tdew-anomaly regression coefficients should vary smoothly with day-of-year (low second derivative), with no sharp discontinuities except near major regime transitions (e.g., wet-season onset).
- Compared to absolute-value regression, anomaly regression should reduce spatially coherent bias patterns tied to elevation and distance-to-coast because those effects are largely absorbed by climatology.

- Replacing day-of-year windowing with a low-order harmonic representation of coefficient seasonality (e.g., 1–3 annual harmonics) will match or exceed wide-window performance while being more data-efficient in high-elevation sparse-station areas.
- A hierarchical model with zone-specific smooth seasonal coefficients and partial pooling across adjacent zones (e.g., foothills bridging Andes and Amazon) will outperform strict per-zone fitting without sacrificing physical plausibility.

- If coefficient seasonality shows abrupt jumps at specific dates (high curvature), then broad windows should underperform a regime-switch or narrow-window model; broad-window superiority would be unexplained.
- If anomaly regression does not improve skill relative to absolute regression when evaluated on held-out years, then the claimed conditioning mechanism is not operating (or climatology estimation is too noisy).

- The provided evidence does not include Peru-specific quantitative diagnostics (e.g., window-width sweep curves, per-zone error metrics), so this theory cannot directly cite those results; it infers mechanisms from analogous methods in the evidence set.

paper-d1411b123812126c1115ca70a6fee252cc.displayLabel: An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1)

s2Metadata.title: An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1)
s2Metadata.abstract: Abstract. Meteorological time series with 1 h time steps are required in many applications in geoscientific modelling. These hourly time series generally cover shorter periods of time compared to daily meteorological time series. We present an open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST). This software package is written in Python and comprises simple methods to temporally downscale (disaggregate) daily meteorological time series to hourly data. MELODIST is capable of disaggregating the most commonly used meteorological variables for geoscientific modelling including temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind speed, and shortwave radiation. In this way, disaggregation is performed independently for each variable considering a single site without spatial dependencies. The algorithms are validated against observed meteorological time series for five sites in different climates. Results indicate a good reconstruction of diurnal features at those sites. This makes the methodology interesting to users of models operating at hourly time steps, who want to apply their models for longer periods of time not covered by hourly observations.

paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062.displayLabel: Improving Subseasonal Forecasting in the Western U.S. with Machine Learning

s2Metadata.title: Improving Subseasonal Forecasting in the Western U.S. with Machine Learning
s2Metadata.abstract: Water managers in the western United States (U.S.) rely on longterm forecasts of temperature and precipitation to prepare for droughts and other wet weather extremes. To improve the accuracy of these longterm forecasts, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) launched the Subseasonal Climate Forecast Rodeo, a year-long real-time forecasting challenge in which participants aimed to skillfully predict temperature and precipitation in the western U.S. two to four weeks and four to six weeks in advance. Here we present and evaluate our machine learning approach to the Rodeo and release our SubseasonalRodeo dataset, collected to train and evaluate our forecasting system. Our system is an ensemble of two nonlinear regression models. The first integrates the diverse collection of meteorological measurements and dynamic model forecasts in the SubseasonalRodeo dataset and prunes irrelevant predictors using a customized multitask feature selection procedure. The second uses only historical measurements of the target variable (temperature or precipitation) and introduces multitask nearest neighbor features into a weighted local linear regression. Each model alone is significantly more accurate than the debiased operational U.S. Climate Forecasting System (CFSv2), and our ensemble skill exceeds that of the top Rodeo competitor for each target variable and forecast horizon. Moreover, over 2011-2018, an ensemble of our regression models and debiased CFSv2 improves debiased CFSv2 skill by 40-50% for temperature and 129-169% for precipitation. We hope that both our dataset and our methods will help to advance the state of the art in subseasonal forecasting.

paper-55c337acba10da6961c31c4504f3748b86.displayLabel: Exploring Design Choices for Autoregressive Deep Learning Climate Models

s2Metadata.title: Exploring Design Choices for Autoregressive Deep Learning Climate Models
s2Metadata.abstract: Deep Learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in medium-range weather prediction but often fail to maintain physically consistent rollouts beyond 14 days. In contrast, a few atmospheric models demonstrate stability over decades, though the key design choices enabling this remain unclear. This study quantitatively compares the long-term stability of three prominent DL-MWP architectures - FourCastNet, SFNO, and ClimaX - trained on ERA5 reanalysis data at 5.625{\deg} resolution. We systematically assess the impact of autoregressive training steps, model capacity, and choice of prognostic variables, identifying configurations that enable stable 10-year rollouts while preserving the statistical properties of the reference dataset. Notably, rollouts with SFNO exhibit the greatest robustness to hyperparameter choices, yet all models can experience instability depending on the random seed and the set of prognostic variables

paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940.displayLabel: An Environmental Data Set for Vector-Borne Disease Modeling and Epidemiology

s2Metadata.title: An Environmental Data Set for Vector-Borne Disease Modeling and Epidemiology
s2Metadata.abstract: Understanding the environmental conditions of disease transmission is important in the study of vector-borne diseases. Low- and middle-income countries bear a significant portion of the disease burden; but data about weather conditions in those countries can be sparse and difficult to reconstruct. Here, we describe methods to assemble high-resolution gridded time series data sets of air temperature, relative humidity, land temperature, and rainfall for such areas; and we test these methods on the island of Madagascar. Air temperature and relative humidity were constructed using statistical interpolation of weather station measurements; the resulting median 95th percentile absolute errors were 2.75°C and 16.6%. Missing pixels from the MODIS11 remote sensing land temperature product were estimated using Fourier decomposition and time-series analysis; thus providing an alternative to the 8-day and 30-day aggregated products. The RFE 2.0 remote sensing rainfall estimator was characterized by comparing it with multiple interpolated rainfall products, and we observed significant differences in temporal and spatial heterogeneity relevant to vector-borne disease modeling.

paper-3feaf818b6139218c4989732c69b2c1d7d.displayLabel: Improvement of reference crop evapotranspiration estimates using limited data for the Brazilian Cerrado

s2Metadata.title: Improvement of reference crop evapotranspiration estimates using limited data for the Brazilian Cerrado
s2Metadata.abstract: : Evapotranspiration (ET) is a key component of the hydrological cycle. Therefore, adequately estimating it is crucial to improving water resource planning and management. One of the most affordable methods of estimating ET is first to estimate reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo) and later associate it to crop and soil coefficients. The FAO Kc-ETo approach can be used only when ETo is computed with the FAO Penman-Monteith equation. However, low data availability may restict the equations used to estimate ETo. In this study, we assess and calibrate common methods used to estimate ETo under such conditions of limited data availability. Based on the annual calibration, the Makkink (NSE = 0.85) outperformed the Priestley-Taylor (NSE = 0.73), Hargreaves-Samani (NSE = 0.56), and Penman-Monteith temperature approach (NSE = 0.58). The seasonal calibration of parameters showed no significant improvement to the methods assessed ( Δ NSE ≤ 0.01), except for the Priestley-Taylor ( Δ NSE = 0.06). The performance of temperature-based equations was particularly limited due to the performance of the equation adopted to estimate global solar radiation. Thus, improving the representation of global solar radiation for limited data availability can also play a key role in improving ETo prediction.

content.title: Daily dew-point persistence improves reconstruction skill

content.text: Including yesterday’s dew point usually improves today’s dew point estimate, especially in humid regions.
**Supporting evidence:**

- MELODIST H3 reconstructs humidity time series using explicit dependence between consecutive days (linear interpolation between daily dew-point values), reflecting the practical usefulness of day-to-day persistence assumptions.  <paper entityId="paper-d1411b123812126c1115ca70a6fee252cc005bde" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="195922148" artifactId="extraction-result-20#uuid-e20.2">Förster et al., 2016</paper>

- AutoKNN demonstrates that lagged anomalies of the target variable improve skill in climate-variable prediction, supporting the general principle that persistence terms are informative.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.1">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

- WeatherBench studies show that autoregressive modeling of atmospheric variables benefits from training protocols that manage error growth, implying that persistence is a powerful but delicate signal in iterative prediction.  <paper entityId="paper-55c337acba10da6961c31c4504f3748b8641c0a3" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="278327193" artifactId="extraction-result-17#uuid-e17.0">Gallusser et al., 2025</paper>

content.title: Iterative gap-filling drift amplification through AR-lag feedback

content.text: Filling long missing periods by iteration can amplify errors into unrealistic spikes.
**Supporting evidence:**

- WeatherBench reports degenerate/exploding autoregressive rollouts in some model configurations/seeds, attributing failures to error accumulation in iterative prediction; multi-step training reduces this instability.  <paper entityId="paper-55c337acba10da6961c31c4504f3748b8641c0a3" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="278327193" artifactId="extraction-result-17#uuid-e17.4">Gallusser et al., 2025</paper>

- AutoKNN and MultiLLR are explicitly autoregressive/lag-informed in their general design philosophy (lagged anomalies and similarity over preceding anomaly sequences), which implies the possibility of error propagation when iterated beyond their validated horizon.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.1">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

- This law/statement was logically inferred (abduction) by combining (i) the existence of autoregressive rollout instability under iteration (WeatherBench) with (ii) the use of AR lags in reconstruction; no Peru-specific extreme-dewpoint diagnostic is in the evidence set.

content.title: Thermodynamic plausibility constraint for reconstructed dew point

content.text: Dew point should not be meaningfully higher than air temperature; if it is, cap it (or cap RH) to avoid supersaturation artifacts.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Chabot-Couture reports that interpolated dew point can exceed interpolated air temperature, producing RH>100%, and suggests users may cap RH at 100%; they also note kriging overshoot/instability when neighbors disagree.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- MELODIST uses the Magnus saturation vapor pressure formula and inversion as the thermodynamic mapping between T, RH, and Tdew; this implies that RH>100% corresponds to Tdew>T and motivates QC/constraints when such states appear from reconstruction or data errors.  <paper entityId="paper-d1411b123812126c1115ca70a6fee252cc005bde" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="195922148" artifactId="extraction-result-20#uuid-e20.4">Förster et al., 2016</paper>

- PMT/FAO-56 workflows compute ea from Tdew via the saturation vapor pressure relation, reinforcing that dew point is physically constrained through vapor-pressure thermodynamics in operational practice, even when estimated from limited data.  <paper entityId="paper-3feaf818b6139218c4989732c69b2c1d7d81cae3" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="250155510" artifactId="extraction-result-18#uuid-e18.0">Althoff et al., 2022</paper>

- If long missing stretches are filled iteratively using AR dew-point lags, the frequency of extreme high-Tdew outliers will increase with gap length; if instead the method is run one-step with observed lags (or periodically reset when observations appear), extreme outliers will largely disappear.
- Adding a plausibility constraint (e.g., enforce RH≤100% via Magnus or enforce Tdew≤Tair+ε) will strongly reduce the count of extreme high dew points while changing median error metrics only slightly if the artifacts are rare.
- Regions with higher humidity persistence (humid lowlands) will gain more median skill from AR lags but will also show greater tail sensitivity during iterative gap filling without constraints.

- Training the reconstruction explicitly for multi-step stability (minimizing k-step-ahead errors, analogous to multi-step objectives in WeatherBench) will reduce extreme-dewpoint artifacts even without hard clipping, by damping unstable feedback through lags.
- Applying constraints in vapor-pressure space (cap ea to a climatologically plausible percentile of saturation vapor pressure at a temperature proxy) will preserve spatial gradients better than simple temperature-space clipping.

- If extreme dew points persist when reconstruction is performed strictly one-step using observed dew-point lags (no iterative feedback), then AR drift is not the primary cause and the failure likely originates in the Tmin→Tdew mapping or Tmin data artifacts.
- If extreme values occur even with no AR terms (pure contemporaneous regression), then the AR-feedback mechanism is not necessary for failure and cannot explain the artifacts.
- If applying RH/Tdew plausibility constraints does not reduce extremes, either the extremes are physically real or the temperature field used for constraints is inconsistent/biased relative to the dew-point field.

- The evidence set does not include the actual Peru reconstruction outputs (maps/time series of >35°C artifacts, the AR-lag structure used, or how gaps were filled), so the theory cannot directly verify the proposed Amazon late-dry-season localization mechanism; it offers a general failure mechanism consistent with autoregressive iteration.

artifacts.description: In late dry season, nights can be warm without being equally humid. A Tmin-based model trained with broad seasonal pooling can then overestimate dew point in that regime, and if it uses dew-point lags to fill gaps, those errors can compound into rare extreme spikes localized to that place and season.

content.title: Regime-dependent Tmin–Tdew mapping causes seasonal sign changes in bias

content.text: The Tmin–dew-point relationship changes between wet and dry regimes; if a model blends regimes, it can become too humid in late dry season.
**Supporting evidence:**

- FAO-56 baseline (Tdew ≈ Tmin) is treated as often violated; deviations depend on season and meteorological controls (wind, evapotranspiration humidification, cloudiness), implying regime dependence rather than a universal identity.  <paper entityId="paper-3feaf818b6139218c4989732c69b2c1d7d81cae3" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="250155510" artifactId="extraction-result-18#uuid-e18.1">Althoff et al., 2022</paper>

- Penman–Monteith temperature approach calibration over the Cerrado finds opposite-signed seasonal corrections: wet season a_T = −0.93°C (Tdew > Tmin) and dry season a_T = +0.57°C (Tdew < Tmin), with annual a_T = −0.42°C. This is direct evidence that Tmin–Tdew coupling changes by regime/season in a tropical seasonal region.  <paper entityId="paper-3feaf818b6139218c4989732c69b2c1d7d81cae3" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="250155510" artifactId="extraction-result-18#uuid-e18.0">Althoff et al., 2022</paper>

- MELODIST documents that simple Tmin-based dew-point assumptions can fail when cloudiness/advection decouple Tmin from ambient moisture; calibrated linear regression (H2) exists precisely to correct site/regime-specific offsets.  <paper entityId="paper-d1411b123812126c1115ca70a6fee252cc005bde" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="195922148" artifactId="extraction-result-20#uuid-e20.0">Förster et al., 2016</paper>

- Chabot-Couture dew-point kriging framework emphasizes day-of-year-dependent parameterization and smoothing of seasonal parameters (31-day windows) to stabilize estimates, highlighting that seasonal structure in humidity-related fields is smooth but meaningful; thus inappropriate pooling can distort seasonally varying relationships.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- This statement was logically inferred by induction from (i) documented wet/dry sign changes in Tmin→Tdew correction in a tropical seasonal biome (Cerrado) and (ii) the general methodological fact that day-of-year smoothing/pooling controls how regimes are blended (as discussed via seasonal smoothing in Chabot-Couture).

content.title: Unconstrained humidity reconstructions can overshoot into physically implausible states

content.text: If you don’t enforce basic humidity physics, statistical models can overshoot and create impossible dew points, especially when the predictor relationship changes seasonally.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Chabot-Couture reports a known failure mode: interpolated dew point can exceed interpolated air temperature, yielding RH>100%; they recommend capping RH at 100% or interpreting as precipitation indication, demonstrating overshoot risk without constraints.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- Magnus formula inversion implies that if derived vapor pressure exceeds saturation at air temperature, computed Tdew will exceed Tair, flagging either supersaturation or (in gridded products) typically an artifact; thus constraint enforcement is physically meaningful.  <paper entityId="paper-d1411b123812126c1115ca70a6fee252cc005bde" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="195922148" artifactId="extraction-result-20#uuid-e20.4">Förster et al., 2016</paper>

- Ensemble ℓ2-normalized averaging and MultiLLR/AutoKNN approaches in the evidence explicitly note they do not impose variable-wise physical constraints; while those papers are not about dew point, they exemplify that skill-driven regression can ignore physical bounds unless added explicitly.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.5">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

content.title: Tail amplification by iterative AR gap filling under biased contemporaneous mapping

content.text: When gap filling reuses yesterday’s predicted dew point, a small seasonal bias can compound across missing stretches into very high spikes.
**Supporting evidence:**

- WeatherBench shows that autoregressive rollouts can become degenerate/exploding due to error accumulation when predictions are iterated forward without stabilizing strategies; this supports the general mechanism of iterative error growth in AR settings.  <paper entityId="paper-55c337acba10da6961c31c4504f3748b8641c0a3" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="278327193" artifactId="extraction-result-17#uuid-e17.4">Gallusser et al., 2025</paper>

- WeatherBench reports that multi-step training (M>1) improves stability relative to single-step, implying that iterative prediction is a distinct regime where errors compound; by analogy, iterative gap filling with AR lags can amplify biases unless explicitly mitigated.  <paper entityId="paper-55c337acba10da6961c31c4504f3748b8641c0a3" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="278327193" artifactId="extraction-result-17#uuid-e17.0">Gallusser et al., 2025</paper>

- This statement was logically inferred by deduction: if (i) seasonal regime bias makes Tdew overestimated in a specific season/region (previous statements) and (ii) AR iteration compounds errors (WeatherBench), then localized seasonal AR gap filling will amplify the upper tail preferentially in that season/region.

- The >35°C reconstructed Tdew events will cluster in time (multi-day runs) and will be more frequent/stronger in grid cells and periods with longer consecutive missing Tdew segments (where recursive AR gap filling is applied), relative to periods with frequent observational anchoring.
- The spikes will be strongly reduced by enforcing a simple physical constraint post hoc (e.g., Tdew ≤ Tmin or Tdew ≤ Tair), converting extreme spikes into saturation-capped values or removing them entirely, with minimal effect on median errors.
- Refitting the Tmin→Tdew mapping with explicit wet vs dry (or antecedent-humidity proxy) stratification within the Amazon lowlands will reduce Aug–Oct spike frequency without necessarily degrading wet-season performance.

- If late-dry-season Tmin is systematically biased high in that region (e.g., due to gridding artifacts), then independent station Tmin or alternate temperature products will show coincident warm biases during Aug–Oct specifically in NE Amazon; correcting Tmin alone would remove the Tdew spikes even without changing the Tdew model.
- If the spikes are partly driven by nonstationarity in the learned mapping (e.g., analog years disproportionately drawn from anomalous recent years), then restricting training to a stationary subperiod or adding a trend term will measurably reduce the spikes while preserving average skill.

- Remove AR dew-point lag predictors (or disable recursive use of predicted Tdew as input during gap filling). If >35°C spikes persist at similar frequency/magnitude, AR tail amplification is not necessary and the primary issue lies in the contemporaneous Tmin→Tdew mapping or Tmin artifacts.
- Diagnose whether spikes coincide with implied supersaturation: compute RH from reconstructed Tdew and an independent Tair estimate using the Magnus relation. If spikes do not produce RH near/above 100% (given plausible Tair), then the values may be physically plausible and the 'unphysical' label (and this theory) would need revision.
- Fit separate models for late dry season (Aug–Oct) versus rest-of-year within the Amazon zone, holding window widths fixed. If the Aug–Oct-specific model still generates spikes, regime blending is unlikely to be the dominant cause.

- The provided evidence set contains no direct observations or cited studies on Amazon Aug–Oct drought/biomass-burning aerosol effects on nighttime Tmin and humidity, so any aerosol/entrainment/soil-moisture mechanism remains speculative in this corpus.

artifacts.description: Nighttime minimum temperature only tracks dew point when the nighttime temperature is controlled by moisture and clouds. Coast, mountains, and rainforest often have different nighttime controls, so zone-specific models work better than one-size-fits-all rules, and mountains need altitude-aware structure to stay realistic.

paper-3feaf818b6139218c4989732c69b2c1d7d.displayLabel: Improvement of reference crop evapotranspiration estimates using limited data for the Brazilian Cerrado

s2Metadata.title: Improvement of reference crop evapotranspiration estimates using limited data for the Brazilian Cerrado
s2Metadata.abstract: : Evapotranspiration (ET) is a key component of the hydrological cycle. Therefore, adequately estimating it is crucial to improving water resource planning and management. One of the most affordable methods of estimating ET is first to estimate reference crop evapotranspiration (ETo) and later associate it to crop and soil coefficients. The FAO Kc-ETo approach can be used only when ETo is computed with the FAO Penman-Monteith equation. However, low data availability may restict the equations used to estimate ETo. In this study, we assess and calibrate common methods used to estimate ETo under such conditions of limited data availability. Based on the annual calibration, the Makkink (NSE = 0.85) outperformed the Priestley-Taylor (NSE = 0.73), Hargreaves-Samani (NSE = 0.56), and Penman-Monteith temperature approach (NSE = 0.58). The seasonal calibration of parameters showed no significant improvement to the methods assessed ( Δ NSE ≤ 0.01), except for the Priestley-Taylor ( Δ NSE = 0.06). The performance of temperature-based equations was particularly limited due to the performance of the equation adopted to estimate global solar radiation. Thus, improving the representation of global solar radiation for limited data availability can also play a key role in improving ETo prediction.

paper-d1411b123812126c1115ca70a6fee252cc.displayLabel: An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1)

s2Metadata.title: An open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST v0.1.1)
s2Metadata.abstract: Abstract. Meteorological time series with 1 h time steps are required in many applications in geoscientific modelling. These hourly time series generally cover shorter periods of time compared to daily meteorological time series. We present an open-source MEteoroLOgical observation time series DISaggregation Tool (MELODIST). This software package is written in Python and comprises simple methods to temporally downscale (disaggregate) daily meteorological time series to hourly data. MELODIST is capable of disaggregating the most commonly used meteorological variables for geoscientific modelling including temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind speed, and shortwave radiation. In this way, disaggregation is performed independently for each variable considering a single site without spatial dependencies. The algorithms are validated against observed meteorological time series for five sites in different climates. Results indicate a good reconstruction of diurnal features at those sites. This makes the methodology interesting to users of models operating at hourly time steps, who want to apply their models for longer periods of time not covered by hourly observations.

paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940.displayLabel: An Environmental Data Set for Vector-Borne Disease Modeling and Epidemiology

s2Metadata.title: An Environmental Data Set for Vector-Borne Disease Modeling and Epidemiology
s2Metadata.abstract: Understanding the environmental conditions of disease transmission is important in the study of vector-borne diseases. Low- and middle-income countries bear a significant portion of the disease burden; but data about weather conditions in those countries can be sparse and difficult to reconstruct. Here, we describe methods to assemble high-resolution gridded time series data sets of air temperature, relative humidity, land temperature, and rainfall for such areas; and we test these methods on the island of Madagascar. Air temperature and relative humidity were constructed using statistical interpolation of weather station measurements; the resulting median 95th percentile absolute errors were 2.75°C and 16.6%. Missing pixels from the MODIS11 remote sensing land temperature product were estimated using Fourier decomposition and time-series analysis; thus providing an alternative to the 8-day and 30-day aggregated products. The RFE 2.0 remote sensing rainfall estimator was characterized by comparing it with multiple interpolated rainfall products, and we observed significant differences in temporal and spatial heterogeneity relevant to vector-borne disease modeling.

paper-7989b73600c90b993f7f95e950264be5aa.displayLabel: STEAD: a high-resolution daily gridded temperature dataset for Spain

s2Metadata.title: STEAD: a high-resolution daily gridded temperature dataset for Spain
s2Metadata.abstract:
Abstract. Using 5520 observatories covering the whole territory of
Spain (about 1 station per 90 km2 considering the whole period), a
daily gridded maximum and minimum temperature was built covering a period
from 1901 to 2014 in peninsular Spain and 1971 to 2014 in the Balearic and Canary
Islands. A comprehensive quality control was applied to the original data,
and the gaps were filled on each day and location independently. Using the
filled data series, a grid of 5 km × 5 km spatial resolution was created by
estimating daily temperatures and their corresponding uncertainties at each
grid point. Four daily temperature indices were calculated to describe the
spatial distribution of absolute maximum and minimum temperature, number of
frost days and number of summer days in Spain. The southern plateau showed
the maximum values of maximum absolute temperature and summer days, while
the minimum absolute temperature and frost days reached their maximums at
the northern plateau. The use of all the available information, the complete
quality control and the high spatial resolution of the grid allowed for an
accurate estimate of temperature that represents a precise spatial and
temporal distribution of daily temperatures in Spain. The STEAD dataset is
publicly available at https://doi.org/10.20350/digitalCSIC/8622 and can be
cited as Serrano-Notivoli et al. (2019).

paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062.displayLabel: Improving Subseasonal Forecasting in the Western U.S. with Machine Learning

s2Metadata.title: Improving Subseasonal Forecasting in the Western U.S. with Machine Learning
s2Metadata.abstract: Water managers in the western United States (U.S.) rely on longterm forecasts of temperature and precipitation to prepare for droughts and other wet weather extremes. To improve the accuracy of these longterm forecasts, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) launched the Subseasonal Climate Forecast Rodeo, a year-long real-time forecasting challenge in which participants aimed to skillfully predict temperature and precipitation in the western U.S. two to four weeks and four to six weeks in advance. Here we present and evaluate our machine learning approach to the Rodeo and release our SubseasonalRodeo dataset, collected to train and evaluate our forecasting system. Our system is an ensemble of two nonlinear regression models. The first integrates the diverse collection of meteorological measurements and dynamic model forecasts in the SubseasonalRodeo dataset and prunes irrelevant predictors using a customized multitask feature selection procedure. The second uses only historical measurements of the target variable (temperature or precipitation) and introduces multitask nearest neighbor features into a weighted local linear regression. Each model alone is significantly more accurate than the debiased operational U.S. Climate Forecasting System (CFSv2), and our ensemble skill exceeds that of the top Rodeo competitor for each target variable and forecast horizon. Moreover, over 2011-2018, an ensemble of our regression models and debiased CFSv2 improves debiased CFSv2 skill by 40-50% for temperature and 129-169% for precipitation. We hope that both our dataset and our methods will help to advance the state of the art in subseasonal forecasting.

content.text: Tmin predicts dew point best when nighttime temperature changes mainly because the air is wetter or cloudier, and worst when Tmin changes mainly because of radiation, advection, or terrain effects. So you get better dew points if you fit different relationships by climate regime and season.
**Supporting evidence:**

- FAO-56 baseline and Cerrado calibration show that Tdew≈Tmin is not generally valid and that the Tmin–Tdew offset changes by season: wet season requires negative a_T (Tdew often > Tmin) while dry season requires positive a_T (Tdew slightly < Tmin). This demonstrates regime/season dependence of Tmin→Tdew coupling and motivates stratification/tuning.  <paper entityId="paper-3feaf818b6139218c4989732c69b2c1d7d81cae3" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="250155510" artifactId="extraction-result-18#uuid-e18.0">Althoff et al., 2022</paper>

- MELODIST humidity disaggregation framework explicitly treats Tdew=Tmin as a simplistic baseline (H1) and introduces a calibrated linear regression (H2: Tdew=a*Tmin+b), indicating that site/regime-specific offsets and slopes improve realism over the identity assumption.  <paper entityId="paper-d1411b123812126c1115ca70a6fee252cc005bde" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="195922148" artifactId="extraction-result-20#uuid-e20.0">Förster et al., 2016</paper>

- MELODIST H3 validation shows strong climate dependence of humidity reconstruction skill (e.g., Rio de Janeiro performs best; Ny-Ålesund performs extremely poorly with r≈0.02 and NSE<0), supporting that diurnal/nocturnal controls can invalidate simple Tmin-based humidity assumptions in certain regimes.  <paper entityId="paper-d1411b123812126c1115ca70a6fee252cc005bde" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="195922148" artifactId="extraction-result-20#uuid-e20.2">Förster et al., 2016</paper>

- Chabot-Couture et al. build dew-point fields by removing seasonality (Fourier harmonics), modeling day-of-year-varying spatial structure, and applying a day-of-year-dependent dew-point lapse rate, emphasizing that both season and geography/altitude control dew-point behavior and must be represented for accuracy.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- PMT/FAO discussion attributes Tmin–Tdew mismatch to missing drivers (wind/advection, evapotranspiration humidification, cloudiness), consistent with the claim that when Tmin variability is not governed by moisture state, Tmin is a weak dew-point proxy.  <paper entityId="paper-3feaf818b6139218c4989732c69b2c1d7d81cae3" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="250155510" artifactId="extraction-result-18#uuid-e18.0">Althoff et al., 2022</paper>

content.title: Elevation-conditioned mean-state necessity for mountainous plausibility

content.text: In mountains, you need an altitude-aware baseline for dew point; Tmin anomalies alone usually can’t create realistic humidity gradients and terrain contrasts.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Chabot-Couture et al. explicitly correct dew point to zero altitude, krige anomalies, and then reapply a day-of-year-dependent dew-point lapse rate, indicating that altitude structure is fundamental to reconstructing plausible dew-point fields.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- Chabot-Couture report that interpolated dew point can exceed air temperature (RH>100%) and recommend user capping/interpretation, illustrating that unconstrained statistical interpolation can violate physical plausibility without careful structure/constraints; terrain/elevation handling is part of their mitigation strategy.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- STEAD temperature reconstruction (not dew point) shows errors increase with elevation and uses altitude and distance-to-coast as covariates, supporting the general principle that complex terrain requires explicit elevation-aware modeling to avoid spatially structured bias.  <paper entityId="paper-7989b73600c90b993f7f95e950264be5aaf91f40" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="284273775" artifactId="extraction-result-14#uuid-e14.0">Serrano‐Notivoli et al., 2019</paper>

content.title: Broad day-of-year pooling as a ‘smooth coupling parameter’ indicator

content.text: If very wide seasonal windows work best, it means the Tmin–dew-point relationship changes gradually through the year and you need lots of samples to estimate it reliably.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Chabot-Couture smooths day-of-year-dependent variogram and lapse-rate parameters using 31-day windows (median then mean) explicitly to stabilize noisy day-of-year fits, demonstrating the variance-reduction rationale and the assumption of smoothly varying seasonal structure.  <paper entityId="paper-bdadb06d28eb745d3e3062df4d42382940d8bad3" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="17774932" artifactId="extraction-result-15#uuid-e15.0">Chabot-Couture et al., 2014</paper>

- MultiLLR and related localized regression frameworks use day-of-year pooling windows (e.g., 56-day windows in the SubseasonalRodeo context) to balance seasonal locality with sample size, illustrating the general principle that broad pooling can improve robustness when parameters vary smoothly with DOY.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.0">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

- AutoKNN uses seasonally restricted training for precipitation (56-day DOY window) but not for temperature, and observes analogs for temperature drawn across months (nonstationarity/trends), reinforcing that the benefit of DOY locality depends on whether the target relationship is strongly seasonal versus smoothly varying or dominated by other factors.  <paper entityId="paper-0a4d4f24f508f9df37e4a155e394f6f062951732" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="52308154" artifactId="extraction-result-19#uuid-e19.1">Hwang et al., 2018</paper>

- If you estimate Tmin→Tdew regression coefficients separately by climate zone, the humid-lowland (Amazon-like) zone should show higher Tmin–Tdew explained variance and stronger short-lag persistence in Tdew than arid-coastal or high-elevation zones (detectable via residual autocorrelation and regression R^2).
- A calibrated linear model (Tdew=a*Tmin+b) fitted per zone should outperform the identity baseline (Tdew=Tmin) more in regimes with strong seasonal shifts in coupling (e.g., wet vs dry season), consistent with FAO/PMT seasonal a_T differences.
- Adding an explicit elevation-conditioned mean state (e.g., lapse-rate-based correction or altitude-dependent climatology) should reduce spatially coherent moisture-gradient artifacts over mountains more than it reduces pointwise random error.

- A single unified model that uses an inferred ‘nocturnal regime index’ derived from temperature-only features (e.g., diurnal temperature range as a proxy for radiative control/cloudiness) could match or exceed explicit zone-splitting while remaining physically interpretable; success would imply regime classification can be learned implicitly from temperature structure.
- Post-processing with a soft physical constraint (penalize Tdew exceeding contemporaneous air temperature, or penalize RH>100% implied by Magnus inversion) may improve plausibility in complex terrain without materially degrading RMSE/MAE—impactful if it prevents localized overshoots while keeping skill.

- If a non-zoned model with identical day-of-year smoothing and AR structure matches zoned performance and yields similar residual diagnostics, then the ‘control hierarchy’ explanation for zone stratification is weakened (zone differences would be mostly statistical/sample-size effects).
- If adding elevation conditioning (e.g., lapse-rate correction) does not improve any plausibility metric over mountains (e.g., reduces frequency of RH>100% or unrealistic ridge moisture), then elevation may not be the limiting factor at the product resolution; the theory’s second law would be challenged.
- If the empirically optimal day-of-year window width differs wildly year-to-year with no stability, then the interpretation of wide windows as reflecting smooth physical evolution is weakened (could indicate nonstationarity or data artifacts).

- This theory does not specifically explain the reported failure mode of unphysically high reconstructed dew points (>35°C) confined to the NE Amazon and Aug–Oct; explaining that spatiotemporal localization requires an additional mechanism (e.g., late-dry-season decoupling plus tail amplification in AR multi-step reconstruction).
